Cell and gene therapy’s next bottleneck is custody of proof

Cell and gene therapy manufacturing is usually framed as a physical scaling problem. Developers need vector yield, cleanroom capacity, qualified raw materials, release-testing throughput and treatment-center slots. These constraints remain real, but solving them often creates a second problem.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-14 · 14 min read

In brief

  • 4 CMC deficiencies sent KRESLADI through a complete-response cycle.
  • 249 days took CASGEVY from BLA submission to FDA approval.
  • 3 sites required a product-specific CASGEVY comparability bridge.
  • 37 regenerative-medicine standards were FDA-recognized through 2025.
  • 2028 is the horizon for KRESLADI’s longest cited CMC commitment.

The factory is only the first gate

source visual

AstraZeneca Cell Therapy Manufacturing Center (54499867408)

A new facility, larger production scale, replacement supplier or revised analytical method can weaken the link between the product used to generate historical evidence and the product that will reach patients. The sponsor must then prove that earlier nonclinical and clinical results remain interpretable.

This is best understood as a sequential regulatory gate, not the dominant bottleneck across the sector. Developers encounter it precisely because they have routed around a more visible constraint by changing the manufacturing system. The underlying task is regulatory custody of proof: the sponsor must measure the relevant difference, establish its consequence, preserve its provenance and submit evidence it is legally entitled to use.

FDA is already trying to reduce unnecessary duplication. Its May 2026 CMC-flexibility guidance is final and allows more flexible approaches to process validation, specifications and other filing requirements. Its June 2026 prior-knowledge guidance remains a draft. That proposal would allow scientifically justified reuse of internal knowledge, public evidence, consortium work and selected third-party information across genome-editing programs.

The policy direction is therefore lower duplication, not lower proof. The biologics-license holder still owns the regulatory conclusion and must demonstrate why reused evidence applies to the particular product.

A comparability bridge preserves the meaning of old evidence

A batch record documents what happened to one lot. A defensible comparability system must explain why results from one process, site or material remain relevant after the system changes.

That requires links among material genealogy, equipment, facilities, operators, process parameters, analytical methods, method versions, reference standards, critical quality attributes, deviations, stability observations and clinical use. Each conclusion must remain traceable to validation protocols, side-by-side studies, transfer results, risk assessments and regulator correspondence.

The core causal chain is straightforward:

Manufacturing change → possible product-attribute change → analytical evaluation → comparability conclusion → decision on historical evidence.

The difficult step is analytical resolution. FDA’s cell and gene therapy comparability draft illustrates the problem with an assay whose coefficient of variation is approximately 20%: such a method cannot reliably distinguish a meaningful product difference of 5%. A beautifully organized evidence system cannot compensate for a measurement system that is too noisy to answer the regulatory question.

Legal custody matters as well. Third-party knowledge may be useful, but 21 CFR 601.2 limits broad incorporation by reference of core biological manufacturing information in a BLA. The plausible architecture is not an open, cross-sponsor evidence network. It is a sponsor-controlled evidence core connected to selective, permissioned external sources.

Eight products show six different outcomes

The public record does not reveal one uniform comparability hurdle. It shows a range of outcomes: successful bridging, bounded intermediate differences, historical-evidence bypasses, remediation cycles, facility handoffs and migration to clinical or commercial constraints.

Figures are drawn from FDA and EMA assessment records and the relevant sponsor disclosures.

CASGEVY and LYFGENIA show what a successful bridge looks like. CASGEVY’s original comparability criteria were not sufficiently justified, so FDA reviewed supplemental analysis before accepting pooled evidence across facilities. LYFGENIA shows that failure to establish equivalence at every intermediate stage does not necessarily invalidate the final product. FDA accepted the totality of downstream controls and functional evidence. (CASGEVY FDA review) (LYFGENIA FDA review)

KEBILIDI demonstrates another route: bypass rather than repair. Lots used in a supportive study were not analytically comparable with the current process, but the pivotal study used material representative of commercial manufacturing. FDA could therefore rely less heavily on the disputed historical bridge. The product still carried postapproval work, including reassessment of limits after ten commercial lots. (KEBILIDI FDA review)

KRESLADI shows the cost of failing at more basic levels. Its first review cycle identified four critical CMC deficiencies involving identity-assay validation, stability, mycoplasma sampling and sterility methodology. The subsequent review accepted selected evidence generated with representative or structurally similar materials, but approval still carried commitments extending through December 2028. (KRESLADI FDA review)

The realized clocks show when the gate becomes expensive

CASGEVY moved from BLA submission to approval in 249 calendar days. KEBILIDI took 243 days. These cases show that a manufacturing bridge does not automatically create a long, visible review delay.

KRESLADI occupied the opposite end of the range. It took 968 days from the initial BLA submission to approval, including a complete response and resubmission. The interval from complete response to approval was 650 days; the resubmission-to-approval interval was 181 days.

Those figures should not be attributed entirely to comparability. KRESLADI’s deficiencies included assay validity, stability, sampling and sterility—problems that a better data architecture could organize but not solve.

BREYANZI reveals a different pattern. Comparability, vector testing, potency and manufacturing-version questions recurred across several years of interactions. A substantial manufacturing and facility submission in May 2020 was treated as a major amendment and added three months to the review clock. FDA’s public record does not separate how much of that extension arose from comparability, manufacturing completeness or facility readiness. (BREYANZI FDA review)

The defensible conclusion is narrow. Evidence continuity can remain a small task when the sponsor quickly bounds a change. It can stretch across review cycles when analytical methods, specifications, stability, sterility or facility execution remain unsettled.

The horizon also extends beyond approval. KRESLADI’s longest cited CMC commitment runs through December 2028. KEBILIDI’s next specification reassessment depends on producing ten commercial lots rather than reaching a fixed date. Evidence continuity is therefore likely to remain a recurring gate through at least 2028, even if other constraints dominate many products.

Measurement assurance sets the technical floor

The deepest shared constraint is not document preparation. It is measurement assurance joined to governed provenance.

A reusable result needs a defined measurand, a known method version, traceable reference material, quantified uncertainty and reproducibility across laboratories. Without those properties, the sponsor cannot know whether an observed difference belongs to the product, the method, the reference standard or the transfer process.

The standards base is expanding. FDA’s recognized regenerative-medicine list reached 37 standards through 2025: 14 dated 2023, nine dated 2024 and 14 dated 2025. These standards cover a heterogeneous set of analytical, transport, cellular-product and data domains. They do not supply universal acceptance criteria for every capsid, cargo, potency mechanism, cell source or manufacturing change. (FDA recognized standards)

One 2026 NIST-led interlaboratory study reported vial-to-vial variation of approximately 0.1% to 5% for candidate AAV material and 2% to 25% for candidate lentiviral-vector material. The 25% figure is not an industry-wide LVV variability rate. It is evidence that even proposed common anchors can carry substantial material-specific uncertainty. (NIST interlaboratory study)

ATCC provides a more tangible scarcity signal. Its VR-1616 rAAV2 reference material is limited to three vials per customer per year. That constraint applies to one specific product, not to all gene therapy standards, but it illustrates how reference-material availability can ration validation and interlaboratory work. (ATCC VR-1616)

Control remains distributed, but the sponsor keeps responsibility

The sponsor controls the filing and the regulatory conclusion. It does not control every useful evidence object.

CDMOs may hold process-transfer history, qualified personnel, facility experience and platform methods. Analytical laboratories may control validated assays, reference standards and method-transfer performance. Software providers can connect manufacturing genealogy, deviations, change control and submission commitments. Standards bodies and regulators determine which measurements and evidence structures carry scientific or legal weight.

This distribution creates switching costs. Moving a method, laboratory, supplier or manufacturing site can itself trigger validation, side-by-side testing and regulatory reassessment. An incumbent provider may therefore earn recurring testing revenue, manufacturing fees, software subscriptions or qualification-driven customer retention.

The economics remain unproven. Public records do not disclose comparability-specific pricing, backlog, margins, authorization fees or segment revenue. The acquisitions of Aldevron, Brammer Bio and Cognate BioServices valued complete operating companies—including capacity, personnel, materials and growth prospects—not a separately identifiable comparability asset.

The same caution applies to software. BIOVIA markets process genealogy and batch comparison; Veeva controls quality and regulatory workflows; IDBS and Alchemi support governed document generation. These functions align with the evidence-continuity problem, but published productivity percentages remain vendor claims. No independent evidence in the record shows that a graph-like deployment reduced repeated studies, regulatory questions or review duration.

The most plausible commercial outcome is therefore bundling. Evidence-lineage functions become embedded in existing LIMS, MES, QMS, regulatory systems, laboratory contracts and CDMO relationships rather than forming a standalone “comparability graph” market.

Commercialization hands the bottleneck downstream

Regulatory evidence can preserve the option to launch. It cannot guarantee that patients will be treated.

Vertex reported $42.9 million of CASGEVY revenue in the first quarter of 2026. Following the July 2026 pediatric label expansion, the company reported more than 75 activated U.S. treatment centers and approximately 5,500 additional eligible children. Those figures show substantial infrastructure formation, but an activated center is capacity—not throughput. The decisive measures are collections, released lots, infusions per center, payer-authorization time and patient attrition before conditioning. (Vertex Q1 2026)

ROCTAVIAN demonstrates the extreme version of this handoff. BioMarin withdrew the product from the market on February 23, 2026 after failing to identify a qualified buyer. BEQVEZ’s European authorization was withdrawn for commercial reasons before launch, while ZYNTEGLO’s German withdrawal followed failed reimbursement negotiations. (ROCTAVIAN withdrawal) (BEQVEZ EMA record)

These outcomes do not make comparability irrelevant. They define its role more precisely. Evidence continuity preserves regulatory and lifecycle options; treatment-center execution, reimbursement, clinical confidence and demand determine how much of that option becomes revenue.

The closest base rate is ICH Q5E

The closest historical precedent is ICH Q5E, the comparability framework for biotechnology products. As protein analytics matured, regulators increasingly accepted manufacturing changes without requiring sponsors to repeat clinical development.

The mechanism is the same today: determine whether historical safety and efficacy evidence remains applicable after a process change.

The starting conditions are different. Cell and gene therapies involve living cells, complex vectors, product-specific potency mechanisms, small datasets and less mature common standards. Vaccine-platform experience during 2020 and 2021 also showed how prior platform knowledge can compress development and change evaluation, but edited cells, AAV and lentiviral products retain greater product-specific uncertainty.

The base rate therefore suggests eventual relief rather than permanent scarcity. Better methods, reference materials and regulatory experience could turn comparability into routine compliance. The unresolved question is how quickly that transition will occur and whether suppliers can earn durable rents before it does.

The strongest counterargument narrows the thesis

The strongest argument against the thesis is that the industry may not need a new infrastructure category at all.

FDA has already issued final CMC-flexibility guidance. KEBILIDI shows that a sponsor can bypass an unsuccessful historical bridge by using current-process pivotal evidence. LYFGENIA and HEMGENIX show that conventional analytical packages and regulator interactions can resolve complex differences. Existing QMS, laboratory, manufacturing and regulatory systems can absorb evidence-lineage functions.

Downstream evidence is even more challenging. Product withdrawals and low utilization indicate that reimbursement, clinical confidence, treatment burden and demand may control realized value more directly than manufacturing evidence.

That argument is persuasive. It defeats the broad claim that comparability is the master bottleneck or that a machine-readable graph is required for acceptance.

The narrower claim survives: manufacturing changes repeatedly create a sponsor-controlled evidence-continuity obligation. That obligation produces recurring analytical, validation, data-governance and postmarketing work, but economic capture will probably remain fragmented across incumbent systems and service providers.

What to watch

  • September 1, 2026: FDA’s prior-knowledge guidance remains draft when the regular comment period closes.
  • Next two Vertex quarters: CASGEVY revenue exceeds $42.9 million in at least one filing.
  • December 31, 2027: One FDA or EMA review accepts prior evidence with an explicit product-specific condition.
  • December 31, 2027: CMS publishes its first CGT Access Model evaluation report.
  • December 31, 2028: An official source reports the status of KRESLADI’s longest cited CMC commitment.
